title: Android TV Box Bought From Amazon Comes Pre-Installed With Malware
content:
#### Description
Recently, systems security consultant Daniel Milisic discovered that an Android TV box purchased from Amazon was pre-loaded with persistent, sophisticated malware baked into its firmware. The T95 streaming device uses an Android 10-based ROM signed with test keys and the ADB (Android Debug Bridge) open over Ethernet and WiFi. This is a suspicious configuration as ADB can be used to connect to devices for unrestricted filesystem access, command execution, software installation, data modification, and remote control. 

While analyzing the DNS request in Pi-hole, Milisic discovered that the device was attempting to connect to several IP addresses associated with active malware.  Milisic believes the malware installed on the device is a strain that resembles 'CopyCat,' a sophisticated Android malware first discovered by Check Point in 2017. This malware was previously seen in an adware campaign where it infected 14 million Android devices to make its operators over $1,500,000 in profits.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/news/2023/01/preinstalled-malware-infested-t95-tv-box-from-amazon
2. https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/android-tv-box-on-amazon-came-pre-installed-with-malware/
3. https://github.com/DesktopECHO/T95-H616-Malware

#### Publication Date
January 30, 2023

#### Author(s)
Nathan Collier  
Bill Toulas  
Daniel Milisic

enhanced.Incident: T95 TV Box Pre-installed Malware
enhanced.Root cause: The primary root cause behind this incident is the presence of pre-installed malware on the T95 TV box, specifically through a malicious launcher APK (DGBLauncher) that loads and executes a Trojan Downloader embedded within a Corejava classes.dex file. The T95 TV box was rooted out-of-the-box, allowing malware to operate with elevated privileges. *The device runs Android 10 OS signed with test keys* (https://securityaffairs.com/140866/security/t95-android-tv-box-malware.html). *The malware was discovered by Daniel Milisic, who created a script to nullify the payload and stop its communication with the C2 server* (https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/android-tv-box-on-amazon-came-pre-installed-with-malware/). *The malware targets devices running AllWinner H616/H618 & RockChip RK3328 processors* (https://github.com/DesktopECHO/T95-H616-Malware). *Another malware, Adups, was also found on the device* (https://hackread.com/amazon-android-tv-box-malware/). *The malware was found on seven TV boxes: T95, T95Z, T95MAX, X88, Q9, X12PLUS, MXQ Pro 5G, and J5-W tablet* (https://www.wired.com/story/android-tv-streaming-boxes-china-backdoor/).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: The specific threat actor or group responsible for this malware is not identified.
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: The victims are consumers who purchased the T95 TV box from Amazon, AliExpress, and other e-commerce platforms. *The compromised devices are in homes, businesses, and schools across the US* (https://www.wired.com/story/android-tv-streaming-boxes-china-backdoor/).
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: The incident was reported on January 30, 2023.
MITRE TTPs: T1071.001: Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
T1505.003: Server Software Component: Web Shell
enhanced.Impact: The impact is the potential exposure of sensitive information and unauthorized access to the network. The financial losses are not specified, but the presence of the Trojan Downloader indicates that the compromised devices could be used for further malicious activities, like click fraud or additional malware downloads. *The malware was deeply baked into the ROM, making it highly persistent* (https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/android-tv-box-on-amazon-came-pre-installed-with-malware/). *The malware includes a Stage-1 and Stage-2 payload system, which communicates with C2 servers like adc.flyermobi.com and ycxrldow.com* (https://github.com/DesktopECHO/T95-H616-Malware). *It was found reaching addresses associated with malware campaigns and redirected C2 server DNS queries to Pi-hole* (https://securityaffairs.com/140866/security/t95-android-tv-box-malware.html). *Multiple layers of malware were identified using tools like nethogs and tcoflow* (https://hackread.com/amazon-android-tv-box-malware/). *Human Security identified advertising fraud and residential proxy services linked to the compromised devices* (https://www.wired.com/story/android-tv-streaming-boxes-china-backdoor/).
Mitigation: Secure the device by performing a factory reset.
Go to the Gear icon for settings.
Navigate to 'More Settings'.
Select 'Device Preferences'.
Scroll down to 'Reset' and follow the instructions.
Remove the pre-installed malware using adb commands:
Install adb on your computer.
Enable 'Developer Mode' and 'USB debugging' on the T95 TV box.
Connect the T95 TV box to your computer using a USB-A to USB-A cable.
Open a terminal and uninstall the malicious launcher:
```bash
adb devices
adb shell pm uninstall -k --user 0 com.swe.dgbluancher
Install an alternative, legitimate TV launcher from a trusted source.
Remove and prevent the reinstallation of Corejava:
Gain root access and enter the shell:
```bash
adb root
adb shell
Remove the Corejava directory and create an immutable file to prevent its recreation:
```bash
rm -rf /data/system/Corejava
touch /data/system/Corejava
chmod 000 /data/system/Corejava
busybox chattr +i /data/system/Corejava
Monitor the device for any suspicious activity.

Internal checks: Setting1: Check for the presence of com.swe.dgbluancher package.
Setting2: Monitor for the creation of /data/system/Corejava directory.
Setting3: Ensure the device is not rooted unless for security research purposes.
External scanning: Monitor network traffic for suspicious outbound connections.
Look for traffic to known malicious URLs associated with the Corejava classes.dex file.
*VirusTotal detected the malware in 13 out of 61 AV engine scans* (https://hackread.com/amazon-android-tv-box-malware/).

IoCs: MD5 of Malicious classes.dex file: F9802B1168D5832D32C229776CD9B9AA
MD5 of Malicious Launcher APK: EB850022E4269BB1DAB9FC5D2B0B734F

title: Recent TZW Campaigns Revealed As Part of GlobeImposter Malware Family
content:
#### Description
Since 2017, campaigns delivering GlobeImposter have continued to proliferate even though the ransomware has only evolved slightly. GlobeImposter is most often delivered via phishing email as an attachment or a link to a malicious attachment. The payloads are typically distributed via 7zip or traditional zip file archives. The archives often include a JavaScript (.js) file that downloads and executes the GlobeImposter payload.

More recent campaigns from within the past three years still tend to follow this formula.

GlobeImposter has also been distributed as a later-stage infection within some well-known botnets. For example, in 2017 GlobeImposter was distributed via the Necurs botnet. This occurred as part of multiple spam campaigns that also included 7zip archives and followed the execution flow previously described.

AhnLab’s research revealed a ransomware campaign they referred to as “TZW” with victims in South Korea. The name is derived from the first 3 characters of the TOR-based victim portal. A closer look suggests that “TZW” samples represent a new variant of the GlobeImposter family.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://www.sentinelone.com/blog/recent-tzw-campaigns-revealed-as-part-of-globeimposter-malware-family/

#### Publication Date
February 15, 2023

#### Author(s)
Jim Walter

enhanced.Incident: TZW Ransomware Campaigns and GlobeImposter Malware Family
enhanced.Root cause: The root cause behind the incident appears to be a phishing campaign that successfully delivered GlobeImposter ransomware via malicious email attachments. The phishing emails contained 7zip archives with JavaScript files that downloaded and executed the GlobeImposter payload. Additionally, the malware infrastructure was misconfigured, exposing Apache Server Status Pages and indicating shared hosting environments. *The TZW ransomware, propagating with the version info marked as 'System Boot Info', was created in a .NET format and includes a loader and the actual ransomware data within it* (https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/46812/). *SentinelOne’s analysis reveals TZW ransomware is a variant of GlobeImposter, sharing the same infrastructure and functionality* (https://www.deepwatch.com/labs/cyber-intel-brief-feb-15-22-2023/). *GlobeImposter is also distributed via blank slate spam, exploits, and fake updates* (https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/win.globeimposter#:~:text=GlobeImposter%20is%20a%20ransomware%20application,mimics%20the%20Globe%20ransomware%20family.).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: The threat actors behind the GlobeImposter malware family, potentially related to TA505 (also known as GOLD TAHOE).
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: The targeted victims include South Korean organizations as identified in the TZW ransomware campaign.
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: The blog post mentions this was observed in February 2023, with ongoing campaigns since 2016.
MITRE TTPs: T1027/002 – Obfuscated Files or Information: Software Packing
T1547/001 – Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
enhanced.Impact: The exact number of records or financial losses is not specified, but the impact includes data encryption and potential data loss due to ransomware. *Files are encrypted with the TZW file extension* (https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/46812/). *The ransomware may prevent system restoration and execution of Anti-Virus solutions* (https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/win.globeimposter#:~:text=GlobeImposter%20is%20a%20ransomware%20application,mimics%20the%20Globe%20ransomware%20family.).
Mitigation: Employ robust email filtering to block phishing emails.
Educate employees about the risks of phishing and how to recognize suspicious emails.
Implement endpoint protection solutions, such as SentinelOne Singularity™, to detect and prevent ransomware.
Regularly back up data and store backups offline to prevent ransomware from encrypting them.
Configure servers securely and avoid exposing unnecessary services to the internet.

Apply patches and updates promptly to mitigate vulnerabilities. *Use anti-malware software like AhnLab V3, which detects and blocks the malware using various detection points* (https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/46812/).

Internal checks: Setting1: Apache Server Status should not be publicly accessible.
Setting2: Ensure proper authentication is configured for sensitive pages.
Setting3: Regularly review server configurations and access controls.
External scanning: Open HTTP/S port with accessible Apache Server Status Page.

title: Raspberry Robin Detected ITW Targeting Insurance & Financial Institutes In Europe
content:
#### Description
Security Joes incident response team has learned that hacking groups are using a new version of Raspberry Robin to attack financial institutes in Europe.

In the latest iteration, the malware protection mechanism has been upgraded to deploy at least five layers of protection before the malicious code is deployed, including a first-stage packer to obscure the code of the next stages of the attack followed by a shellcode loader.

The next three layers include a second-stage loader DLL, intermediate shellcode, and finally the shellcode downloader. This complex framework makes the worm more difficult to detect and simultaneously eases lateral movement through networks.  The research also indicated Raspberry Robin operators have began to collect more data about their victims than earlier reported.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://www.securityjoes.com/post/raspberry-robin-detected-itw-targeting-insurance-financial-institutes-in-europe
2. https://www.darkreading.com/threat-intelligence/raspberry-robin-worm-highly-complex-upgrade

#### Publication Date
January 2, 2023

#### Author(s)
Felipe Duarte  
Charles Lomboni  
Shlomit Chkool  
Nathan Eddy

enhanced.Root cause: Exploitation of compromised QNAP servers used as Command and Control (C2) servers.

enhanced.Organization/industry/location: Insurance and financial institutions in Europe, with a focus on Spanish and Portuguese-speaking organizations.
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: Not explicitly stated in the blog, but incidents were documented as occurring in the month leading up to January 2023.
MITRE TTPs: T1071.001: Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
enhanced.Impact: The blog does not specify the exact number of records leaked or the financial losses.
Mitigation: Monitor and update defense mechanisms to detect and block the Raspberry Robin framework.
Ensure proper security controls on QNAP servers, including regular updates and patches.
Implement network segmentation to limit the spread of malware.
Educate employees on phishing and social engineering tactics to prevent initial infection vectors.
Regularly audit and monitor system logs for unusual activities or connections to known malicious IP addresses.
Detailed Steps for mitigation: **Update Security Systems**: Ensure that antivirus and endpoint detection systems are updated with the latest signatures to detect Raspberry Robin.
**Secure QNAP Servers**: Apply the latest firmware updates, restrict access to the management interface, and disable unnecessary services.
**Network Segmentation**: Isolate critical systems from general user networks to prevent lateral movement.
**Employee Training**: Conduct regular training sessions on recognizing phishing attempts and suspicious email attachments.
**System Audits**: Implement regular audits of system and network logs to identify and respond to abnormal activities promptly.

Internal checks: Ensure QNAP servers are updated with the latest firmware. – In platform
QNAP management interface should not be exposed to the external internet. – Inside VMs
Implement strong authentication mechanisms for accessing QNAP devices. – Inside VMs
External scanning: Port (8080) open
Detect traffic to known C2 IPs, e.g., 85.56.236[.]45

title: StopRansomware Royal Ransomware  CISA
content:
#### Description
The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) released this joint Cybersecurity Advisory (CSA) to disseminate known Royal ransomware IOCs and TTPs identified through FBI threat response activities as recently as January 2023.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-061a


#### Publication Date
March 2, 2023

#### Author(s)
CISA
FBI

enhanced.Incident: BlackSuit (Royal) Ransomware
enhanced.Root cause: The root cause includes multiple vectors: phishing emails with malicious attachments or links, RDP compromise, vulnerable public-facing applications, and brokered access via harvested VPN credentials. Actors used legitimate software and open-source tools like Cobalt Strike, SystemBC, Rubeus, and SharpHound for command and control, persistence, lateral movement, and data exfiltration. *The threat actor's command and control traffic was proxied through CloudFlare to conceal their Cobalt Strike server* (https://thedfirreport.com/2024/08/26/blacksuit-ransomware/). *They also exploited AnyDesk and MobaXterm tools for remote access and persistence* (https://socradar.io/dark-web-profile-blacksuit-ransomware/). *The group also used Gootloader malware and penetration testing tools like Ursnif/Gozi* (https://www.hipaajournal.com/cisa-fbi-royal-blacksuit-ransomware/). *BlackSuit actors disable antivirus software and extract large amounts of data before ultimately deploying the ransomware* (https://sprysquared.com/cisa-and-fbi-release-update-to-advisory-royal-ransomware-actors-rebrand-ad-blacksuit-august-7-2024/).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: BlackSuit (formerly known as Royal) Ransomware
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: Multiple sectors and industries across the US, including the Communications Sector, Critical Manufacturing Sector, and Healthcare and Public Health Sector. *BlackSuit has targeted over 350 victims globally* (https://socradar.io/dark-web-profile-blacksuit-ransomware/). *Notable victims include the City of Dallas, TX* (https://www.hipaajournal.com/cisa-fbi-royal-blacksuit-ransomware/). *Octapharma, a leading blood plasma provider, was attacked in April 2024, disrupting operations across 35 states in the U.S.* (https://sprysquared.com/cisa-and-fbi-release-update-to-advisory-royal-ransomware-actors-rebrand-ad-blacksuit-august-7-2024/). *Kershaw County School District and Henry County School system were also targeted* (https://sprysquared.com/cisa-and-fbi-release-update-to-advisory-royal-ransomware-actors-rebrand-ad-blacksuit-august-7-2024/).
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: The advisory does not provide specific start and end dates for the attacks but mentions activities observed from September 2022 onwards, with recent updates as of August 2024. *BlackSuit first emerged in May 2023* (https://socradar.io/dark-web-profile-blacksuit-ransomware/).
MITRE TTPs: Initial Access: T1566 (Phishing), T1566.001 (Spearphishing Attachment), T1566.002 (Spearphishing Link), T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application), T1021.001 (Remote Services: RDP), T1133 (External Remote Services)
Persistence: T1133 (External Remote Services), T1078 (Valid Accounts), *T1547.001 (Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder)* (https://thedfirreport.com/2024/08/26/blacksuit-ransomware/)
Privilege Escalation: T1078 (Valid Accounts), T1078.002 (Domain Accounts)

Defense Evasion: T1070.001 (Clear Windows Event Logs), T1119 (Automated Collection), T1484.001 (Group Policy Modification), T1562.001 (Disable or Modify Tools), *T1055 (Process Injection)* (https://thedfirreport.com/2024/08/26/blacksuit-ransomware/)
Credential Access: T1078 (Valid Accounts), T1003.001 (LSASS Memory)
Command and Control: T1105 (Ingress Tool Transfer), T1572 (Protocol Tunneling)
enhanced.Impact: Over $500 million USD in ransom demanded, with individual ransom demands ranging from $1 million to $10 million USD. The largest individual ransom demand was $60 million. Financial and operational impacts include data encryption, exfiltration, and potential public release of sensitive data. *BlackSuit also leveraged double extortion tactics* (https://www.hipaajournal.com/cisa-fbi-royal-blacksuit-ransomware/). *BlackSuit actors have shown a readiness to negotiate ransom amounts* (https://sprysquared.com/cisa-and-fbi-release-update-to-advisory-royal-ransomware-actors-rebrand-ad-blacksuit-august-7-2024/).
Mitigation: Implement a recovery plan to maintain and retain multiple copies of sensitive data in a secure, segmented location.
Require compliance with NIST standards for password policies, including longer passwords, password managers, and account lockouts.
Keep all operating systems, software, and firmware up to date, prioritizing the patching of known vulnerabilities.
Require multi-factor authentication (MFA) for administrator accounts and critical services.
Segment networks to prevent lateral movement.
Use network monitoring tools to detect abnormal activity and potential ransomware traversal.
Regularly update and enable real-time detection for antivirus software on all hosts.
Implement secure logging collection and storage practices.
Review domain controllers, servers, and workstations for new or unrecognized accounts.
Audit user accounts with administrative privileges and configure access controls according to the principle of least privilege.
Disable unused ports and enforce email security policies.
Disable macros by default and consider adding email banners for external emails.
Implement time-based access for admin-level accounts and disable command-line scripting activities.
Maintain offline backups of data and ensure backups are encrypted and immutable.
*Consider HC3 alerts for healthcare-related threats* (https://www.hipaajournal.com/cisa-fbi-royal-blacksuit-ransomware/).
*Review updated advisory and implement suggested measures* (https://sprysquared.com/cisa-and-fbi-release-update-to-advisory-royal-ransomware-actors-rebrand-ad-blacksuit-august-7-2024/).

Internal checks: Monitor for unusual activity on RDP, SSH, and other remote access services.
Monitor for unusual file creation or modification in directories like C:\Temp\, C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Roaming\, C:\ProgramData\, etc.
Monitor for execution of batch scripts and use of tools like Mimikatz, RClone, Cobalt Strike.
External scanning: External connections from known malicious IP addresses.

title: Emotet Resumes Spam Operations, Switches to OneNote
content:
#### Description
Following its initial return to spamming operations, Emotet was leveraging heavily padded Microsoft Word documents in an attempt to evade detection. By leveraging a large number of inconsequential bytes in their documents, they could increase the size of the documents to surpass the maximum file size restrictions that automated analysis platforms like sandboxes and anti-virus scanning engines enforce.

The initial emails were consistent with what has been commonly observed from Emotet in recent years. They typically contained an attached ZIP archive containing a Microsoft Word document.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://blog.talosintelligence.com/emotet-switches-to-onenote/

#### Publication Date
March 22, 2023

#### Author(s)
Edmund Brumaghin  
Jaeson Schultz

enhanced.Incident: Emotet Resumes Spam Operations
enhanced.Root cause: The root cause behind the incident is the use of malicious OneNote documents and heavily padded Microsoft Word documents containing macros and scripts. The vulnerability exploited is the lack of proper email filtering and endpoint protection to detect these malicious attachments. *Healthcare Sector* (https://www.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/emotet-the-enduring-and-persistent-threat-to-the-hph-tlpclear.pdf).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: Emotet Botnet, *GOLD CABIN*, *MUMMY SPIDER* (https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/win.emotet)
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: General targets (not specified), potentially multiple industries and locations due to the widespread nature of Emotet campaigns. *HPH Sector (Healthcare and Public Health)* (https://www.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/emotet-the-enduring-and-persistent-threat-to-the-hph-tlpclear.pdf).
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: March 7, 2023 – Ongoing (as of the latest update on March 22, 2023)
MITRE TTPs: T1071.001 - Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
enhanced.Impact: The exact number of devices or financial losses is not specified, but Emotet campaigns typically aim to infect as many systems as possible, leading to significant network disruptions and potential data breaches. *Credential Theft and Data Exfiltration* (https://www.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/emotet-the-enduring-and-persistent-threat-to-the-hph-tlpclear.pdf).

Mitigation.Email Filtering: Implement advanced email filtering to block suspicious attachments and links.
Mitigation.Endpoint Protection: Use endpoint protection solutions that can detect and block macro-based malware and malicious scripts.
Mitigation.User Training: Conduct regular training sessions to educate users on recognizing phishing emails and suspicious attachments.
Mitigation.Macro Settings: Disable macros by default in Microsoft Office applications and enforce strict policies on the use of macros.
Mitigation.Network Segmentation: Segment the network to limit the spread of malware.
Mitigation.Regular Updates: Ensure all systems and software are regularly updated with the latest security patches.

Detailed Steps for Mitigation: Configure Email Gateways: Block emails with executable content inside attachments (e.g., .js, .vbs, .wsf).
Deploy Advanced Threat Protection: Use solutions like Cisco Secure Endpoint, Cisco Secure Email, and Cisco Secure Firewall.
Implement Policies: Use Group Policy Objects (GPO) to disable macros in Office files received from the internet.
User Awareness Training: Regularly simulate phishing attacks to train employees on identifying suspicious emails.
Monitor Network Traffic: Use tools like Cisco Secure Network Analytics to identify unusual network activities.

Detection Signature.Signature name: Emotet Phishing Email with OneNote/Word Attachment
Internal checks: Setting1: Scan incoming emails for known Emotet IOCs.
Setting2: Block emails with attachments of specific file types (e.g., .one, .docm).
Setting3: Monitor for execution of macros and scripts from Office documents.
External scanning: Monitor email server logs for indicators of Emotet-related email patterns.
Use IDS/IPS to detect malicious VBA macro execution and script downloads.

IoCs.Indicators of Compromise (IOCs) associat: No specific IoCs found in the provided document text itself.

enhanced.Additional Information: Emotet, historically a banking malware, has evolved to serve as infrastructure for distributing other malware like *Trickbot* and facilitating *Ryuk ransomware* attacks (https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/win.emotet). Emotet's new campaign bypasses Microsoft's macro block by sending spam emails with malicious OneNote files containing a fake message to trick victims into downloading the malware. Once installed, it gathers email data for expanding the attack campaign. *Qbot as prevalent malware* (https://blog.checkpoint.com/security/march-2023s-most-wanted-malware-new-emotet-campaign-bypasses-microsoft-blocks-to-distribute-malicious-onenote-files/). *VirusTotal spike observed*; *Payload Obfuscation*; *URLs for Emotet payloads* (https://www.esentire.com/blog/pulse-check-on-onenote-for-malware-delivery).

title: Nevada Ransomware Being Distributed in Korea
content:
#### Description
AhnLab Security Emergency response Center (ASEC) discovered cases of the Nevada ransomware being distributed during the team’s internal monitoring. Nevada is a malware written using Rust as its basis and its tendency of adding the “.NEVADA” extension to the files it infects is its defining trait. After encrypting directories, it generates ransom notes with the filename “README.txt” in each directory. These notes contain a Tor browser link for ransom payments.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/50063/

#### Publication Date
March 22, 2023

#### Author(s)
ASEC_SK

enhanced.Incident: Nevada Ransomware Being Distributed in Korea
enhanced.Root cause: The primary vector of the ransomware's distribution is not explicitly mentioned, but common vectors include phishing emails, malicious downloads, or exploiting vulnerabilities in systems. *Support for command-line options enables various encryption methods* (https://asec.ahnlab.com/jp/50048/).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: Not explicitly mentioned, but associated with the Nevada ransomware group and affiliates from the RAMP underground community *affiliates from RAMP underground community* (https://www.resecurity.com/blog/article/nevada-ransomware-waiting-for-the-next-dark-web-jackpot).
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: General targets in Korea.
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: The blog mentions the ransomware being detected on March 16, 2023, *and March 22, 2023* (https://asec.ahnlab.com/jp/50048/). *Updates on January 20th and February 2nd, 2023* (https://www.resecurity.com/blog/article/nevada-ransomware-waiting-for-the-next-dark-web-jackpot). No end date provided.
MITRE TTPs: T1490: Inhibit System Recovery (Volume Shadow Deletion)
T1021.002: Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) (Encrypt Shared Network Folders)
T1083: File and Directory Discovery (Encryption of specific files and directories)
enhanced.Impact: Not explicitly mentioned, but ransomware typically leads to significant data loss and potential financial losses due to ransom payments, operational disruptions, and recovery costs.
Mitigation: Secure Backups: Regularly back up data and ensure that backups are not connected to the network.
Endpoint Protection: Use advanced anti-malware solutions with real-time protection.
Security Awareness Training: Educate employees about phishing and safe internet practices.
Patch Management: Regularly update and patch systems to protect against vulnerabilities.
Network Segmentation: Implement network segmentation to limit the spread of ransomware.
Disable Macros: Disable macros in Office files from unknown sources.
Email Filtering: Use email filtering to block malicious attachments and links.
Least Privilege Principle: Apply the principle of least privilege to limit user access rights.
Firewall and IDS/IPS: Implement robust firewall and intrusion detection/prevention systems.
Detailed Steps for mitigation: Backup Strategy: Implement a 3-2-1 backup strategy (three copies of your data, two on different media, one off-site).
Anti-malware: Deploy and regularly update endpoint protection solutions like V3.
Patching: Automate patch management to ensure all software is up-to-date.
Training: Conduct regular security training sessions for employees.
Macros: Disable Office macros by default and only allow them for trusted documents.
Email Security: Use advanced email security solutions to filter out malicious emails.
Access Controls: Regularly review and adjust user permissions to ensure minimal access.

Internal checks: Setting1: Monitor for creation of ransom notes with filenames like “README.txt”
Setting2: Detect file extensions being renamed to “.NEVADA”
Setting3: Monitor for unusual process behavior, such as self-deletion commands.
External scanning: Monitor for command and control (C2) traffic
Scan for unusual network encryption activity

IoCs: Other detection signatures mentioned: File Detection: Ransomware/Win.Nevada.C5391542 (2023.03.06.03), Behavior Detection: Ransom/MDP.Decoy.M1171, Ransom/MDP.Event.M1785

title: New Infostealer LummaC2 Being Distributed Disguised As Illegal Cracks
content:
#### Description
A new Infostealer called “LummaC2” is being distributed disguised as illegal programs such as cracks and keygens. Other malware such as CryptBot, RedLine, Vidar, and RecordBreaker (Raccoon V2) are distributed in a similar manner.  It appears that the LummaC2 Stealer has been available for purchase on the dark web since the beginning of this year, and since March, it has been distributed by a threat group disguised as a crack.  The LummaC2 Stealer was first discovered on March 3rd, and additional distributions were confirmed on the 12th and 20th of the same month, indicating an approximate activity rate of once a week.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/50594/


#### Publication Date
March 27, 2023

#### Author(s)
KDH

enhanced.Incident: LummaC2 Infostealer Distribution

title: SmoothOperator  Ongoing Campaign Trojanizes 3CXDesktopApp in Supply Chain Attack
content:
#### Description
As of Mar 22, 2023 SentinelOne began to see a spike in behavioral detections of the 3CXDesktopApp, a popular voice and video conferencing software product categorized as a Private Automatic Branch Exchange (PABX) platform.  The trojanized 3CXDesktopApp is the first stage in a multi-stage attack chain that pulls ICO files appended with base64 data from Github and ultimately leads to a 3rd stage infostealer DLL. The compromise includes a code signing certificate used to sign the trojanized binaries.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://www.sentinelone.com/blog/smoothoperator-ongoing-campaign-trojanizes-3cx-software-in-software-supply-chain-attack/
2. [CrowdStrike Tracking Active Intrusion Campaign Targeting 3CX Customers](https://ti.defender.microsoft.com/articles/d76f059a/description)


#### Publication Date
March 30, 2023

#### Author(s)

enhanced.Incident: 3CX SmoothOperator Supply Chain Attack
enhanced.Root cause: The root cause includes the compromise of the 3CXDesktopApp software, trojanized with malware. Attackers infiltrated the supply chain introducing malicious code into legitimate application binaries. The compromised code included a trojanized `libffmpeg.dylib` library in the macOS app and a multi-stage attack chain in the Windows app. The attackers employed a *DLL side-loading technique* (https://www.uptycs.com/blog/3cx-supply-chain-attack). *The macOS variant was validly signed by the 3CX developer and notarized by Apple* (https://objective-see.org/blog/blog_0x73.html).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: The campaign is linked to the Lazarus malware family per Mandiant. However, the exact threat actor behind this specific campaign is still under investigation, though CrowdStrike suspects LABYRINTH CHOLLIMA *(https://research.kudelskisecurity.com/2023/03/30/3cx-supply-chain-attack-smoothoperator/)*. *SentinelOne researchers also tracked the activity under the name SmoothOperator* (https://thehackernews.com/2023/03/3cx-desktop-app-targeted-in-supply.html).
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: The incident targeted 3CX, a business communications software company. Victims include 3CX's broad customer base in industries like automotive, food & beverage, hospitality, MSPs, and manufacturing. *3CX claims to have more than 600,000 customers and 12 million users in 190 countries, including well-known names like American Express, BMW, Honda, Ikea, Pepsi, and Toyota* (https://thehackernews.com/2023/03/3cx-desktop-app-targeted-in-supply.html).
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: The attack was detected on March 22, 2023, with analysis and updates continuing through to at least April 24, 2023.
MITRE TTPs: T1059.001: Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell
T1055.002: Process Injection: Portable Executable Injection
T1071.001: Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
T1070.004: Indicator Removal on Host: File Deletion
enhanced.Impact: Potential compromise of up to 600,000 customer companies with 12 million daily users relying on 3CX's software.

Mitigation.Ensure Software Integrity: Implement a robust code-signing process and regularly audit software integrity.
Mitigation.Network Segmentation: Segment the network to limit malware spread.
Mitigation.Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR): Use EDR solutions to monitor and detect suspicious activities on endpoints.
Mitigation.Security Patches: Regularly update and patch software to mitigate known vulnerabilities.
Mitigation.User Training: Train users to recognize phishing and social engineering attacks.
Detailed Steps: Implement strict controls on the software development pipeline to detect unauthorized changes.
Use multi-factor authentication (MFA) to protect access to build systems.
Regularly conduct security assessments and code reviews.
Maintain an up-to-date inventory of all software dependencies and third-party libraries.
Deploy security monitoring tools to detect anomalies in software behavior.

Internal checks: Verify the integrity of `libffmpeg.dylib` in macOS applications.
Monitor for unexpected network connections initiated by 3CXDesktopApp.
Check for unauthorized modifications to the 3CXDesktopApp installation directory.
External scanning: Scan for known malicious domains and IP addresses used by the trojan.
Monitor for suspicious activities and connections to GitHub repositories like `github[.]com/IconStorages/images`.

enhanced.Additional Details: *Cortex XDR, Cortex XSOAR, and Next-Generation Firewall protections were highlighted for blocking malicious activity and preventing further exploitation. The RC4 key used in this attack, 3jB(2bsG#@c7, was noted as previously seen in Labyrinth Chollima activities* (https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/3cxdesktopapp-supply-chain-attack/). Attackers also extracted *MachineGuid* (https://www.uptycs.com/blog/3cx-supply-chain-attack) and used the *RC4 algorithm* (https://www.uptycs.com/blog/3cx-supply-chain-attack) to decrypt data. They targeted popular browsers like Chrome to steal sensitive data *(https://www.uptycs.com/blog/3cx-supply-chain-attack)*.

title: QBot Banker Delivered Through Business Correspondence
content:
#### Description
In early April, Securelist detected a significant increase in attacks that use banking Trojans of the QBot family (aka QakBot, QuackBot, and Pinkslipbot). The malware would be delivered through e-mail letters written in different languages — variations of them were coming in English, German, Italian, and French.  The messages were based on real business letters the attackers had gotten access to, which afforded them the opportunity to join the correspondence thread with messages of their own. As a general rule, such letters would be urging the addressee — under a plausible pretext — to open an enclosed PDF file. As an example, they could be asking to provide all the documentation pertaining to the attached application or to calculate the contract value based on the attached cost estimate.

Qbot’s functionality hardly changed in the past couple of years. As before, the bot is capable of extracting passwords and cookies from browsers, stealing letters from your mailbox, intercepting traffic, and giving operators remote access to the infected system. Depending on the value of the victim, additional malware can be downloaded locally, such as CobaltStrike (to spread the infection through the corporate network) or various ransomware. Or else the victim’s computer can be turned into a proxy server to facilitate redirection of traffic, including spam traffic.

Conduct regular security awareness training for employees to recognize phishing attempts. 3. Enable PowerShell script block logging and monitor logs for suspicious activity. 4. title: 8220 Gang Uses Log4Shell Vulnerability to Install CoinMiner
content:
#### Description
Ahnlab Security Emergency response Center (ASEC) has recently confirmed that the 8220 Gang attack group is using the Log4Shell vulnerability to install CoinMiner in VMware Horizon servers. Among the systems targeted for the attack, there were Korean energy-related companies with unpatched and vulnerable systems, hence being preyed upon by multiple attackers.

Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) is both a remote code execution vulnerability and the Java-based logging utility Log4j vulnerability that can remotely execute a Java object in servers that use Log4j by including the remote Java object address in the log message and sending it.

title: Trigona Ransomware Attacking MS-SQL Servers
content:
#### Description
AhnLab Security Emergency response Center (ASEC) has recently discovered the Trigona ransomware being installed on poorly managed MS-SQL servers. Trigona is a relatively recent ransomware that was first discovered in October 2022, and Unit 42 has recently published a report based on the similarity between Trigona and the CryLock ransomware.

Poorly managed MS-SQL servers typically refer to those that are exposed to external connections and have simple account credentials, rendering them vulnerable to brute force or dictionary attacks. If a threat actor manages to log in, control over the system will be passed to them, allowing them to install malware or execute malicious commands.

Additionally, MS-SQL can be installed on both Windows servers and desktop environments. For example, there are cases where MS-SQL is installed alongside certain ERP and work-purpose solutions during their installation process. Because of this, Windows servers and Windows desktop environments can both be targeted for MS-SQL Server attacks.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/51343/

#### Publication Date
April 16, 2023

#### Author(s)
Sanseo

enhanced.Incident: Trigona Ransomware Attacking MS-SQL Servers
enhanced.Root cause: Poorly managed MS-SQL servers with simple account credentials and exposure to external connections. This vulnerability allows threat actors to perform brute force or dictionary attacks to gain unauthorized access.
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: Trigona ransomware operators. The report also mentioned the use of CLR SqlShell malware, *CryptBot malware* (https://global.ahnlab.com/global/upload/download/asecreport/ASEC%20REPORT_vol.109_ENG.pdf), and the exploitation of *Windows Secondary Logon Service* (https://heimdalsecurity.com/blog/trigona-ransomware-deployed-through-vulnerable-microsoft-sql-servers/). *Malware executed as svcservice.exe service* (https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/microsoft-sql-servers-hacked-to-deploy-trigona-ransomware/#:~:text=%22CLR%20Shell%20is%20a%20type,web%20servers%2C%22%20AhnLab%20says.).
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: *Manufacturing sector* (https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/trigona-ransomware-update/).
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: *Discovered in October 2022* and *active during December 2022* (https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/trigona-ransomware-update/).
enhanced.Impact: The specific number of records or financial losses is not mentioned in the report.

Secure MS-SQL Servers: Ensure MS-SQL servers are not exposed to external connections unnecessarily.
Use strong, complex passwords and change them periodically.
Implement account lockout policies to prevent brute force attacks.

Regularly update and patch MS-SQL servers and underlying OS to mitigate known vulnerabilities. *Consider CVE-2022-26809* (https://global.ahnlab.com/global/upload/download/asecreport/ASEC%20REPORT_vol.109_ENG.pdf).
Use Security Tools: Deploy anti-malware solutions like V3 and keep them updated.
Use firewalls to restrict access to database servers from the outside.
Implement network monitoring to detect unusual activities.
Privilege Management: Restrict high privileges on MS-SQL servers to the minimum necessary.
Regularly review and audit user accounts and their privileges.
Backup and Recovery: Regularly backup data and ensure backups are stored securely and offline.
Test recovery plans to ensure data can be restored quickly in the event of an attack.
*Maintain offline backups and ensure all backup data is encrypted and immutable* (https://www.csk.gov.in/alerts/Trigona_ransomware.html).
*Implement multi-factor authentication for all services and remove unnecessary access to administrative shares* (https://www.csk.gov.in/alerts/Trigona_ransomware.html).

Internal checks.Setting1: MS-SQL Server should not be exposed to external Internet connections.
Internal checks.Setting2: MS-SQL Server account credentials should be complex and changed periodically.
Internal checks.Setting3: Monitor and alert on multiple failed login attempts on MS-SQL Server.

External scanning.Port (1433) open: Check if MS-SQL Server port is open to the public Internet.
External scanning.Brute force attempts: Monitor for multiple failed login attempts within a short time frame.

title: Goldenjackal APT Targets Middle Eastern and South Asian Governments and Diplomatic Entities
content:
#### Description
Researchers at Kaspersky provide an analysis of the activities and tactics employed by the GoldenJackal Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) group. The group has been active since at least 2019 and primarily targets organizations in the Middle East and South Asia. GoldenJackal has a sophisticated and stealthy modus operandi, blending in with legitimate software and using various evasion techniques to avoid detection. They exploit vulnerabilities in popular applications and leverage social engineering techniques for initial access. The group demonstrates advanced capabilities, including custom malware development and the ability to gather sensitive information from compromised systems. GoldenJackal's primary objective appears to be cyber-espionage, with a focus on political, diplomatic, and economic interests in the targeted region.

#### Publication Date
June 19, 2023

#### Author(s)
Giampaolo Dedola

Attackers spread malware through fake Skype installers and malicious Word documents. *GoldenJackal also targeted air-gapped systems using custom toolsets like GoldenHowl, GoldenRobo, and GoldenDealer* (https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/mind-air-gap-goldenjackal-gooses-government-guardrails/). *ESET researchers noted the use of USB-based infiltration* (https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/goldenjackal-exploits-air-gapped/). *JackalControl is a Trojan that allows attackers to remotely manipulate the targeted machine* (https://www.pcrisk.com/removal-guides/26816-jackal-malware).

title: RecordBreaker Infostealer Disguised as a .NET Installer
content:
#### Description
Researchers at AhnLab Security Emergency Response Center have identified a new variant of malware called RecordBreaker, which is disguised as a .NET installer. In the past, malware was distributed as executable files or compressed files containing malicious content. However, this new variant masquerades as a legitimate .NET update installer from the official Microsoft website. When executed in a regular user environment, the malware downloads and executes an encrypted file from the threat actor's server. However, in a virtual environment or analysis sandbox, the malware downloads and executes the legitimate .NET installer instead of the malicious file, making it difficult to detect.

The compressed file containing the malware is designed to deceive users as it includes several normal files and folders. This strategy aims to make the malware appear as a regular file among commonly used files. By doing so, the malware can bypass analysis environments such as sandboxes or VirusTotal. This variant of RecordBreaker differs from previous versions in several ways. It is written in the Rust programming language and has a smaller file size, ranging from 20 to 50 MB compared to the previous bloated versions that were as large as 3 GB. The malware employs various techniques to disrupt analysis, including scanning for virtual environment-related strings, file and folder names, running processes, and system information. Once executed, RecordBreaker steals sensitive information based on the configuration received from the command-and-control (C2) server. It then sends the stolen data to the C2 server before terminating itself. 

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/54658/

#### Publication Date
June 20, 2023

#### Author(s)
AhnLab, KDH

It is mainly distributed in abnormally large sizes with padding added between sections, leading to file sizes between 3 to 7MB compressed and 300 to 700MB decompressed *The changes* (https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/35981/). title: Apple Crimeware  Massive Rust Infostealer Campaign Aiming for macOS Sonoma Ahead of Public Release
content:
#### Description
Security researcher 'iamdeadlyz' reported on multiple fake blockchain games being used to infect both Windows and macOS targets with infostealers, capable of emptying crypto wallets and stealing stored password and browser data. In the case of macOS, the infostealer turned out to be a new malware written in Rust, dubbed “realst”. Building on this previous analysis, SentinelOne identified and analyzed 59 malicious Mach-O samples of realst malware. Among those, SentinelOne discovered some samples are already targeting Apple’s forthcoming OS release, macOS 14 Sonoma.

Realst Infostealer is distributed via malicious websites advertising fake blockchain games with names such as Brawl Earth, WildWorld, Dawnland, Destruction, Evolion, Pearl, Olymp of Reptiles, and SaintLegend. The campaign appears to have links to the earlier PearlLand infostealer. Each version of the fake blockchain game is hosted on its own website complete with associated Twitter and Discord accounts.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://www.sentinelone.com/blog/apple-crimeware-massive-rust-infostealer-campaign-aiming-for-macos-sonoma-ahead-of-public-release/

#### Publication Date
July 25, 2023

#### Author(s)
Phil Stokes

enhanced.Root cause: The primary root cause behind the Realst Infostealer campaign is the use of fake blockchain games to distribute malware. The malicious software is delivered through websites advertising these fake games, which include Mach-O samples targeting macOS systems. The malware takes advantage of social engineering tactics, such as direct messages through social media, to lure victims into downloading and executing the malicious software. *The campaign also involves the distribution of RedLine Stealer* (https://iamdeadlyz.gitbook.io/malware-research/july-2023/fake-blockchain-games-deliver-redline-stealer-and-realst-stealer-a-new-macos-infostealer-malware#realst-stealer-macos). *Some versions of the malware are packaged in Electron apps and native macOS applications* (https://www.tanium.com/blog/cti-roundup-realst-malware-targets-macos-infostealer-malware-sees-exponential-growth/). *The malware is written in the Rust programming language, known for its high performance and memory safety* (https://www.hokanews.com/2023/07/breaking-rust-based-realst-infostealer.html). *The fake blockchain games used include Brawl Earth, WildWorld, Dawnland, Destruction, Olymp of Reptiles, and SaintLegend* (https://www.secureblink.com/cyber-security-news/realst-stealthy-mac-os-infostealer-from-fake-blockchain-games-exposed). *It is distributed through PKG installers and DMG disks containing malicious Mach-O files* (https://www.techradar.com/pro/new-macos-malware-is-after-your-data-and-your-crypto-heres-how-to-stay-safe).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: The exact threat actor(s) behind this campaign is not explicitly identified, but the campaign is linked to earlier PearlLand infostealer activities and *PureLand, which is associated with sandbox malspam* (https://iamdeadlyz.gitbook.io/malware-research/july-2023/fake-blockchain-games-deliver-redline-stealer-and-realst-stealer-a-new-macos-infostealer-malware#realst-stealer-macos). *Our meticulous analysis revealed 16 variants divided into four major families: A, B, C, and D* (https://www.secureblink.com/cyber-security-news/realst-stealthy-mac-os-infostealer-from-fake-blockchain-games-exposed). *Some samples were signed using valid Apple Developer IDs to bypass detection* (https://www.techradar.com/pro/new-macos-malware-is-after-your-data-and-your-crypto-heres-how-to-stay-safe).
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: *The campaign targets macOS users, particularly those with interests in blockchain games and cryptocurrency*. *It also specifically prepares for macOS 14 Sonoma* (https://www.tanium.com/blog/cti-roundup-realst-malware-targets-macos-infostealer-malware-sees-exponential-growth/).
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: The blog post references research from July 2023, indicating the campaign was active around this time.

T1553: Bypass or Subvert Trust Controls (xattr)
T1562: Disable or Modify Tools (sleep, waitpid)
T1639.001: Exfiltration Over Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol (tcp, http)
enhanced.Impact: The campaign has compromised the security of macOS users by stealing sensitive data, including browser data, stored passwords, and cryptocurrency wallet information. The exact number of affected users is not specified, but the distribution of multiple fake games suggests a potentially significant impact. *The malware also exfiltrates data to Telegram channels* (https://www.tanium.com/blog/cti-roundup-realst-malware-targets-macos-infostealer-malware-sees-exponential-growth/). *It operates very stealthily and removes digital traces to evade detection* (https://www.hokanews.com/2023/07/breaking-rust-based-realst-infostealer.html). *Telegram is a target along with Chrome, Firefox, Opera, Brave, and Vivaldi browsers* (https://www.techradar.com/pro/new-macos-malware-is-after-your-data-and-your-crypto-heres-how-to-stay-safe).

Implement robust endpoint protection solutions like SentinelOne, which can detect and prevent the execution of known variants of the Realst infostealer.
Regularly update macOS systems to the latest version to benefit from security patches and improved malware defenses.
Educate users about the risks of phishing and social engineering tactics to reduce the likelihood of falling victim to such campaigns.

Internal checks: Verify if any unauthorized installation of Python scripts like `game.py` and `installer.py` is present.
Monitor for suspicious network traffic to URLs like `167.172.103.83:8080/opened` and `77.91.84.110:5000/send_analytics`.
Check for unexpected creation of directories named 'data' in user home folders or download directories.
External scanning: Identify and block network traffic to the known malicious IP addresses and domains associated with the campaign.

title: Lazarus Group Exploits ManageEngine Vulnerability to Deploy QuiteRAT
content:
#### Description
Cisco Talos discovered the North Korean state-sponsored actor Lazarus Group targeting internet backbone infrastructure and healthcare entities in Europe and the United States. This is the third documented campaign attributed to this actor in less than a year, with the actor reusing the same infrastructure throughout these operations.

In this campaign, the attackers began exploiting a ManageEngine ServiceDesk vulnerability (CVE-2022-47966) five days after PoCs for the exploit were publicly disclosed to deliver and deploy a newer malware threat we track as “QuiteRAT.” Security researchers first discovered this implant in February, but little has been written on it since then.

QuiteRAT has many of the same capabilities as Lazarus Group’s better-known MagicRAT malware, but its file size is significantly smaller. Both implants are built on the Qt framework and include capabilities such as arbitrary command execution.

Lazarus Group’s increasing use of the Qt framework creates challenges for defenders. It increases the complexity of the malware’s code, making human analysis more difficult compared to threats created using simpler programming languages such as C/C++, DOT NET, etc. Furthermore, since Qt is rarely used in malware development, machine learning and heuristic analysis detection against these types of threats are less reliable.

title: SapphireStealer Open-Source Information Stealer Enables Credential and Data Theft
content:
#### Description
SapphireStealer, an open-source information stealer, has been observed across public malware repositories with increasing frequency since its initial public release in December 2022. Information-stealing malware like SapphireStealer can be used to obtain sensitive information, including corporate credentials, which are often resold to other threat actors who leverage the access for additional attacks, including operations related to espionage or ransomware/extortion. In some cases, SapphireStealer appears to be delivered as part of a multi-stage infection process, with threat actors leveraging open-source malware downloaders like FUD-Loader to deliver SapphireStealer to potential victims.

Cisco assess with moderate confidence that multiple entities are using SapphireStealer, who have improved and modified the original code base separately, extending it to support additional data exfiltration mechanisms leading to the creation of several variants.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://blog.talosintelligence.com/sapphirestealer-goes-open-source/

#### Publication Date
August 31, 2023

#### Author(s)
Edmund Brumaghin

It facilitates credential and data theft by exploiting user systems *using DotNetZip* (https://github.com/0day2/SapphireStealer/), and targets device data such as CPU architecture and IP addresses *through multi-stage processes* (https://www.pcrisk.com/removal-guides/27668-sapphirestealer-malware).

These actors aim to steal credentials and sell them for cyber-espionage, ransomware, and identity theft. *Some threat actors have extended SapphireStealer to support added functionality and used anti-detection mechanisms, reflecting an increasing trend* (https://malware.news/t/new-open-source-infostealer-and-reflections-on-2023-so-far/73009).

Use secure email gateways to block phishing attempts and malicious attachments.
Employ web filtering solutions to block access to known malicious sites and IPs.

Detect and alert on the creation of directories like %TEMP%\sapphire\work.
Identify processes attempting to capture screenshots or access browser credential databases.

Look for the presence of hardcoded credentials or PDB paths in executable files.

SapphireStealer is written entirely in C# and supports stealing logs from Chromium browsers* (https://github.com/0day2/SapphireStealer/). *Cisco Talos has observed increasing use of open-source infostealers like SapphireStealer across public malware repositories and underground forums* (https://malware.news/t/new-open-source-infostealer-and-reflections-on-2023-so-far/73009).

The emails contained a malicious CHM file attachment executing JavaScript code running a PowerShell script that fetched and decrypted ctlhost.exe, planting MerlinAgent on victims' devices for lateral movement *The changes* (https://www.bitdefender.com/blog/hotforsecurity/ukraine-warns-of-attacks-targeting-state-organizations-using-open-source-tool-merlin/?srsltid=AfmBOooBYwEy5FIk9EnYjcbH_qWmwHVE360JEtcKNE-2SUpmqnN2kv0U).

title: Beyond the Horizon Traveling the World on Camaro Dragon’s USB Flash Drives
content:
#### Description
In early 2023, Check Point Research conducted an investigation into a malware incident at a European healthcare institution. The malware, attributed to the Chinese-based espionage threat actor Camaro Dragon, spread through infected USB drives. The malware, known as WispRider, had the ability to self-propagate through USB drives and infect networks globally, even if they were not the primary targets. The investigation revealed that Chinese threat actors, including Camaro Dragon, continue to use USB devices as an infection vector.

The malware infection at the European healthcare institution was traced back to an employee who had participated in a conference in Asia and unknowingly brought back an infected USB drive. When the employee connected the USB drive to the hospital's computer systems, the malware spread and infected the network. The incident shed light on a set of tools previously described in an Avast report and linked to Twill Typhoon (TANTALUM), another Chinese threat actor. The malware used a Delphi launcher on the infected USB drives to unleash the main backdoor and infect new drives it encountered.

Further analysis of the malware revealed newer versions of the toolset, including the USB launcher known as HopperTick and the backdoor-infector component called WispRider. These versions combined all the functionality into a single payload and utilized legitimate executables from security software and gaming companies for DLL-side-loading. The malware had undergone significant refactoring and code changes, incorporating C++ language capabilities. The updated malware versions were observed spreading from Southeast Asia to countries like Russia.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://research.checkpoint.com/2023/beyond-the-horizon-traveling-the-world-on-camaro-dragons-usb-flash-drives/

#### Publication Date
June 22, 2023

#### Author(s)
Check Point Research Team

enhanced.Incident: Camaro Dragon USB Flash Drive Malware Campaign
enhanced.Root cause: The incident was primarily caused by the use of infected USB drives. The malware utilized a set of tools, including WispRider and HopperTick, which were able to self-propagate through USB drives and networked storage devices *The changes* (https://social.cyware.com/news/self-propagating-chinese-malware-inadvertently-affects-networked-storage-devices-1d4ab4b2). Vulnerable/misconfigured services included lack of proper endpoint protection, insufficient USB device security policies, and the exploitation of legitimate software components (like Symantec and Vivaldi) to side-load malicious DLLs. The infection originated from an employee who attended an Asian conference and used an infected USB drive. The malware campaign also involved a novel Go-based backdoor called TinyNote, capable of bypassing SmadAV, a popular antivirus software in Southeast Asia *The changes* (https://www.keysight.com/blogs/en/tech/nwvs/2023/07/05/threat-simulator-june-2023-update).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: Camaro Dragon (linked to Chinese-based espionage groups, Mustang Panda, and LuminousMoth); *TinyNote Backdoor* (https://www.keysight.com/blogs/en/tech/nwvs/2023/07/05/threat-simulator-june-2023-update)
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: European healthcare institution, with evidence of infections in Myanmar, South Korea, Great Britain, India, and Russia.
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: Early 2023 (exact dates not specified)
enhanced.Impact: The self-propagating nature of the malware led to widespread infections across multiple countries. The exact number of records or financial losses is not specified.
Mitigation: Enforce strict USB device usage policies, including prohibiting unauthorized USB devices.
Implement endpoint protection solutions to detect and block malware from USB drives.
Regularly update and patch software to prevent exploitation of known vulnerabilities.
Use application whitelisting to prevent unauthorized executables from running.
Conduct regular security awareness training to educate employees on the risks of using external USB devices.
Utilize advanced threat detection solutions like Check Point Harmony Endpoint and Threat Emulation.

Detection Signature.Service: Endpoint Protection (e.g., Check Point Harmony Endpoint)
Detection Signature.Incident: Camaro Dragon USB Flash Drive Malware Campaign

Internal checks.Setting1: Monitor for unauthorized USB device connections
Internal checks.Setting2: Scan for and block execution of files from USB drives
Internal checks.Setting3: Ensure endpoint protection is up to date and configured to block malware

Detection Signature.External scanning: N/A (focus on endpoint monitoring rather than network scanning)

*New Details*: Check Point Incident Response Team (CPIRT) investigated the attack and found that it was perpetrated by Camaro Dragon.
WispRider bypasses SmadAV, a popular antivirus software in Southeast Asia.
The malware is part of a toolset labeled 'SSE'.
*KeySight's ATI Research Center identified the threat* (https://www.keysight.com/blogs/en/tech/nwvs/2023/07/05/threat-simulator-june-2023-update).

title: GuLoader Malware Disguised as Tax Invoices and Shipping Statements
content:
#### Description
AhnLab Security Emergency response Center (ASEC) has identified circumstances of GuLoader being distributed as attachments in emails disguised with tax invoices and shipping statements. The recently identified GuLoader variant was included in a RAR (Roshal Archive Compressed) compressed file. When a user executes GuLoader, it ultimately downloads known malware strains such as Remcos, AgentTesla, and Vidar.

Besides Remcos, GuLoader also downloads and runs malware strains being sold on the Internet such as Formbook and Lokibot. Such malware strains offered for sale are called commodity malware. The threat actor likely uses downloaders such as GuLoader to propagate commercial malware instead of distributing them directly to bypass signature-based detection of security products. In the past, GuLoader was compiled in VisualBasic, and nowadays, it is compiled in NSIS and .NET. Whatever the case may be, its form is constantly being changed during distribution to evade static detection. However, the malware strains being executed in the memory area are commercial malware types such as Remcos, so even if the forms are different, each variant performs the same malicious behaviors.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/55978/

#### Publication Date
August 9, 2023

#### Author(s)
AhnLab_En

enhanced.Incident: GuLoader Malware Campaign
enhanced.Root cause: The root cause behind this incident is the use of malicious email attachments disguised as tax invoices, shipping statements, and spam mails with malicious macros. These emails contain compressed files (RAR) that, when executed, download various malware strains like Remcos, AgentTesla, and Vidar. Notably, Remcos is a Remote Access Trojan (RAT) with keylogging and screenshot capture features. *The changes* (https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/18015/) *Additionally, the campaign relies on bypassing Mark of the Web (MotW) protections and is not mitigated by Smart App Control (SAC) when it's in Evaluation or OFF mode* (https://malwaretips.com/threads/easy-application-control-on-windows.130803/).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: Unknown (The blog post does not specify the threat actor behind this campaign)
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: General Internet users (The blog post does not specify a particular target organization or industry)
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: Not specified in the blog post
enhanced.Impact: The specific number of records or financial losses is not disclosed in the blog post.
Mitigation: **Email Filtering**: Implement advanced email filtering solutions to detect and block malware distributed via email attachments.
**Endpoint Protection**: Utilize endpoint security products that include behavior-based detection to identify and block malicious activities.
**User Training**: Educate users on recognizing phishing emails and the risks of executing unknown attachments.
**Sandbox Analysis**: Use sandbox-based APT solutions to analyze suspicious email attachments before they reach end users.

*Additionally, Easy Application Control (EAC) can be applied to block files originating from the Internet Zone, offering non-invasive protection by allowing popular documents and media files while restricting others* (https://malwaretips.com/threads/easy-application-control-on-windows.130803/).
Detailed Steps for Mitigation: Deploy a robust email security gateway that can filter out emails containing suspicious attachments.
Integrate behavior-based detection mechanisms within endpoint security solutions to detect and mitigate threats like GuLoader.
Conduct regular training sessions to help employees recognize phishing attempts and understand the importance of not opening unknown attachments.
Implement sandbox environments to analyze the behavior of email attachments in a controlled setting, preventing potential malware from reaching the corporate network.

*Utilize Windows built-in applications for email and archive management to maintain Mark of the Web (MotW) and leverage Easy Application Control (EAC) for additional protections* (https://malwaretips.com/threads/easy-application-control-on-windows.130803/).

Detection Signature.Port: N/A (Email systems typically use ports 25, 465, and 587 for SMTP)
Internal checks: Set up rules to flag emails with attachments that match known patterns of GuLoader and other associated malware.
External scanning: Monitor for emails originating from known malicious IP addresses or domains used in GuLoader campaigns.

title: Under Siege Rapid7-Observed Exploitation of Cisco ASA SSL VPNs
content:
#### Description
Rapid7’s managed detection and response (MDR) teams have observed increased threat activity targeting Cisco ASA SSL VPN appliances (physical and virtual) dating back to at least March 2023.  In some cases, adversaries have conducted credential stuffing attacks that leveraged weak or default passwords; in others, the activity Rapid7 observed appears to be the result of targeted brute-force attacks on ASA appliances where multi-factor authentication (MFA) was either not enabled or was not enforced for all users (i.e., via MFA bypass groups). Several incidents Rapid7's managed services teams have responded to ended in ransomware deployment by the Akira and LockBit groups.

There is no clear pattern among target organizations or verticals. Victim organizations varied in size and spanned healthcare, professional services, manufacturing, and oil and gas, along with other verticals. 

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2023/08/29/under-siege-rapid7-observed-exploitation-of-cisco-asa-ssl-vpns/

#### Publication Date
August 29, 2023

#### Author(s)
Rapid7

enhanced.Incident: Exploitation of Cisco ASA SSL VPNs
enhanced.Root cause: Weak or default passwords on Cisco ASA SSL VPN appliances, lack of enforced Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA), and vulnerable VPN configurations. *The issue stems from improper separation of authentication, authorization, and accounting (AAA) in Cisco ASA and FTD* (https://securityaffairs.com/150516/hacking/cve-2023-20269-cisco-asa-e-ftd.html).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: Akira and LockBit ransomware groups, and initial access broker 'Bassterlord'. *The use of LSASS dumps and Living-Off-The-Land Binaries (LOLBins) has been observed* (https://blogs.cisco.com/security/akira-ransomware-targeting-vpns-without-multi-factor-authentication). *Trigona ransomware is also targeting VPNs across the industry* (https://www.techtarget.com/searchsecurity/news/366550138/Cisco-VPNs-under-attack-via-Akira-LockBit-ransomware).
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: Victim organizations varied across healthcare, professional services, manufacturing, and oil and gas, among other verticals.
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: March 2023 – August 2023
enhanced.Impact: Multiple organizations impacted, leading to ransomware deployment in several cases. The exact number of records or financial losses is not specified. *Threat actors use a TOR network site for extortion* (https://blogs.cisco.com/security/akira-ransomware-targeting-vpns-without-multi-factor-authentication).
Mitigation: Ensure default accounts are disabled or passwords are reset from the default.
Enforce MFA across all VPN users, minimizing exceptions to this policy.
Enable logging on VPNs, specifically for Cisco ASA devices.
Monitor VPN logs for authentication attempts from unexpected locations.
Monitor VPN logs for failed authentications, looking for brute forcing and password spraying patterns.
Keep current on patches for security issues in VPNs and other gateway devices.

*Implement Dynamic Access Policies (DAP) and secure default remote access VPN profiles to mitigate CVE-2023-20269 risks* (https://www.secureblink.com/cyber-security-news/ransomware-group-exploit-cisco-vpn-zero-day-vulnerability).

Detection Signature.Incident: Unauthorized access attempts and brute force attacks on Cisco ASA SSL VPNs. *The zero-day vulnerability CVE-2023-20269 impacts Cisco ASA Software Release 9.16 or earlier* (https://securityaffairs.com/150516/hacking/cve-2023-20269-cisco-asa-e-ftd.html).

Internal checks.Setting2: Ensure default and weak passwords are not in use.
Internal checks.Setting3: Enable and monitor detailed logging for VPN access attempts.

IoCs.*Additional observations from Rapid7's M: Rapid7 identified IP addresses linked to AnyDesk remote desktop application.

Newly added entities.*Clientless SSL VPN session* (https://ww: Allows attackers to establish a session without additional authorization.
